Unlike traditional VQA, Embodied Question Answering (EQA) may require an agent to acquire and retain evidence from a 3D environment before answering a natural language query. This semi-systematic survey reviews a core corpus of 72 papers selected from 210 candidates and supplements it with a separate targeted qualitative update comprising 28 additional records identified through July 2026. We use PMRA (Perception\u2013Memory\u2013Reasoning\u2013Action) as an author-developed analytical framework rather than a new robot-control architecture, together with a three-level taxonomy of task formulations, method architectures, and capability dimensions. An audit of the 20 tabulated datasets, with counts recomputed from the accompanying extraction sheet, finds that five permit or require active exploration and only one requires physical object interaction. We also define four architecture-based stages without using publication year as an assignment rule. The qualitative synthesis identifies examples of explicit memory interfaces and question-conditioned information-acquisition mechanisms, but it does not infer their prevalence, temporal growth, or relative importance from publication frequencies. Finally, we discuss four recurring limitations of foundation-model approaches and nine research directions toward 2030.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.3390\/ai7090367","type":"journal-article","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["A Survey of Visual Question Answering for Embodied Robots: Tasks, Methods, and Future Directions"],"author":[{"ORCID":"https:\/\/orcid.org\/0009-0009-0593-3639","authenticated-orcid":false,"given":"Weihan","family":"Shi","sequence":"first","affiliation":[{"name":"Faculty of Data Science, City University of Macau, Macau 999078, China"},{"name":"Hainan International College, Minzu University of China, Lingshui 572423, China"}],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]},{"ORCID":"https:\/\/orcid.org\/0000-0002-6468-8233","authenticated-orcid":false,"given":"Yinlong","family":"Liu","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[{"name":"Faculty of Data Science, City University of Macau, Macau 999078, China"}],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"container-title":["AI"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026,9,15]]},"URL":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.3390\/ai7090367"},{"abstract":"<jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems can produce fluent clinical text, but they remain prone to hallucination: confident answers that are factually wrong or unsupported by any source. In safety-critical medicine this failure mode carries real consequences. This paper presents MedSAFE, a question-answering system that adapts the Self-Discover reasoning framework of Zhou et al. (2024) and constrains all evidence retrieval to three continuously updated, authoritative sources: PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). MedSAFE follows the Self-Discover Select, Adapt, and Implement stages to compose a task-specific reasoning structure, then answers only from retrieved records, exposing the reasoning trace and the citations behind each conclusion. The prototype was evaluated with an LLM-as-a-Judge protocol against two general-purpose assistants (ChatGPT and Gemini) on a set of ten clinical questions of varying difficulty, scored on ten rubric dimensions worth two points each. On a representative anticoagulation question involving nonvalvular atrial fibrillation with stage 5 chronic kidney disease, MedSAFE scored 20 of 20, compared with 17 for Gemini and 15 for ChatGPT, with its largest relative advantages in consistency and safety netting. The results are consistent with the claim that restricting retrieval to vetted, current sources and making the reasoning auditable improves the trustworthiness of clinical answers, at the cost of slower and more narrowly scoped responses. Limitations include a small evaluation set, a single judge model, and reliance on a demonstration rather than a controlled trial.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.7145318","type":"posted-content","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["Implementing Self-Discover Reasoning for Trustworthy Medical Question Answering A Restricted-Retrieval Reasoning System (MedSAFE) for Reducing Hallucination in Clinical Question Answering"],"author":[{"ORCID":"https:\/\/orcid.org\/0009-0003-8239-628X","authenticated-orcid":true,"given":"Simin","family":"Kim","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"vocabulary":"crossref","role":"author"}]}],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"URL":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.2139\/ssrn.7145318"},{"DOI":"10.65528\/9780807775882-005","title":["2 Reasoning Abstractly and Quantitatively"],"author":[{"given":"Marian","family":"Small","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"role":"author","vocabulary":"crossref"}]}],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2010,1,25]]},"container-title":["Teaching Mathematical Thinking"],"is-referenced-by-count":0,"URL":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.65528\/9780807775882-005","type":"book-chapter"}],"items-per-page":10,"query":{"start-index":0,"search-terms":null}}}
